promptText: A URL shortener's non-functional requirements specify a 100:1 read-to-write ratio with relaxed write-side consistency. Why does this ratio, more than the exact QPS numbers, determine the system's architecture?
options: It dictates that nearly every architectural lever — caching, redirect-path latency, and the decision to avoid sharding — must be optimized for the read path, since optimizing the rare write path at the read path's expense would solve the wrong problem
It means the database must be synchronously replicated across every region to keep reads consistent
It determines the exact number of characters needed in the short code, independent of the total number of stored records
It eliminates the need for any caching layer, since reads are already cheap relative to writes
explanation: Because a link is created once but clicked many times, almost every design decision — cache-first reads, a lightweight write path, no premature sharding — follows directly from the read path dominating by two orders of magnitude. The exact QPS numbers mostly just size the infrastructure; a 10x miss on QPS rarely changes which architecture is correct, but getting the ratio itself wrong changes the shape of the whole design.

promptText: Why must a custom-alias request be enforced with a database-level unique constraint on short_code rather than an application-level "look up, then insert if absent" check?
options: Two concurrent requests for the same alias can both pass the lookup before either has written, so only an atomic database-level constraint reliably rejects the second insert regardless of timing
Application-level checks are equally correct but are avoided only because they run slower than a constraint check
A unique constraint is required because the database cannot add an index to a VARCHAR column without one
Database constraints are needed only because custom aliases are longer than generated codes and risk column-length overflow
explanation: A check-then-insert in application code is unsafe under concurrency: two racing requests for the same alias can both observe "not taken" before either writes, letting both through. A database-level unique constraint closes that race because the database itself atomically rejects the second conflicting insert no matter how the requests interleave.

promptText: Why does choosing a 301 (permanent) redirect over a 302 (temporary) one for resolving short codes carry a real product trade-off rather than being an arbitrary implementation detail?
options: A 301 lets browsers and proxies cache the redirect themselves, reducing server load, but it can suppress future requests from the same browser, making reliable per-click analytics harder to capture
A 301 is required whenever the destination URL uses HTTPS, while a 302 is required for HTTP destinations
A 302 permanently removes the short link from the database once it has been issued, while a 301 does not
Browsers refuse to follow a 302 redirect across domains, unlike a 301
explanation: A 301 lets browsers and intermediate proxies cache the redirect themselves, cutting load on the service, but a browser holding a cached 301 may never hit the server again for subsequent clicks, undermining per-click observability. A 302 guarantees every click is seen server-side at the cost of forgoing that browser-level caching, which is a real trade-off worth naming rather than an arbitrary status-code pick.

promptText: In the design's cache-aside read path, why does the write path (shortening a URL) never populate the cache directly?
options: Cache-aside populates the mapping lazily on the first read that misses, keeping the write path simple and avoiding a cache-write cost for links that may never be clicked before their TTL would expire anyway
Redis cannot accept writes from the same service instance that just wrote to the primary database
Writing to the cache synchronously would violate the database's unique constraint on short_code
The write path uses write-through caching exclusively, which by definition excludes any read-triggered cache population
explanation: The design deliberately uses cache-aside, not write-through: the cache fills lazily on first read miss rather than being pre-warmed on write, because most newly created links are not read often enough in their first moments to justify the extra write-path cost of filling the cache on every create. This keeps the already-cheap write path simple and pushes the only real performance work onto the dominant read path.

promptText: Why is a single relational table with one primary-key index (on short_code) sufficient for this system's data model, rather than something requiring joins or secondary indexes?
options: The only access pattern on the hot path is an exact point lookup by short code, with no range scans or joins, so a primary-key index serves it directly without added structure that would go unused
Relational databases cannot support more than one index per table, so a single index is the only option available
A single index is required because VARCHAR primary keys cannot be combined with any other column in the same table
It is sufficient only because the table is expected to remain under one million rows indefinitely
explanation: Every read in this design is a point lookup by exact short code, never a range scan or a complex join, so a plain primary-key index already serves the entire read path's access pattern. Adding more schema structure or a more complex store would add operational cost without serving any access pattern this product actually has.

promptText: For click-count-based link expiry, why is incrementing the click counter asynchronously (via the same event used for analytics) preferable to incrementing it synchronously on every redirect?
options: A synchronous increment on every redirect adds write amplification directly to the hottest path in the system, whereas an async increment accepts a link serving a few requests slightly past its exact limit in exchange for not paying that cost on every read
Asynchronous increments are required because database counters cannot be updated more than once per second
Synchronous increments are impossible because the redirect handler has no access to the database connection pool
Asynchronous incrementing is needed only because click-count expiry is mutually exclusive with date-based expiry
explanation: Date-based expiry is cheap to check inline because it rides along with the already-cached mapping, but a click counter that must increment on every single redirect is exactly the kind of write-amplification you don't want on the hottest path in the system. Driving the increment off the same asynchronous analytics event accepts a small amount of overshoot past the exact click limit in exchange for never paying a synchronous write cost on every read.

promptText: The chapter derives a 6-character base62 short code from a projected 6.08 billion records over 5 years, rejecting 62^5 (~916 million) and choosing 62^6 (~56.8 billion) over 62^7 (~3.5 trillion). What is the reasoning behind picking 6 characters over 7?
options: Six characters is the shortest length that comfortably exceeds the 5-year projected record count without needing a later length migration, while seven would work too but offers far more headroom than the data justifies
Seven characters would exceed the maximum VARCHAR(8) column width enforced by the schema, making six the only valid choice
Six characters is required because base62 encoding only produces even-length strings for integers above one billion
The choice is arbitrary, since both six and seven characters are equally rejected by the collision-avoidance requirement
explanation: 62^6 comfortably covers the projected 6.08 billion records with room to spare, while 62^5 falls short and 62^7 is far more capacity than the estimate calls for. Choosing the shortest length that still comfortably outlives the projection is the concrete, numbers-driven decision the chapter asks for, instead of guessing "6 or 7, doesn't really matter."

promptText: Real high-scale systems like bit.ly reportedly favor a pre-generated key-pool service over base62-encoding an ID at request time. What problem does this approach solve that base62(auto-increment ID) does not?
options: It removes all code generation and collision-avoidance work from the hot write-path request entirely, since uniqueness was already guaranteed when the pool was populated offline, at the cost of operating a separate standing key-generation service
It eliminates the need for a uniqueness constraint on custom aliases, since all codes come from the same pre-generated pool
It allows the system to support content-based deduplication, which base62(auto-increment ID) cannot provide
It removes the need for a cache on the read path, since pre-generated keys are stored in a format that doesn't require lookups
explanation: A pre-generated key pool mints and stores unique codes ahead of time, so the hot write path only has to claim an already-unique row instead of allocating an ID or checking for collisions at request time. The trade-off is operating a second, standalone generator service and pool, which is why it is reserved for write volumes where even ID-allocation contention starts to matter, not adopted by default.

promptText: A single short link suddenly goes viral, receiving tens of thousands of redirects per second. Why does this scenario, counterintuitively, favor this design rather than threaten it, and what real risk remains?
options: A single hot key is the easiest traffic pattern to cache, since repeated requests for the same code are nearly identical, so load barely reaches the database once warm; the real risk is a thundering herd of concurrent misses in the brief window before the key becomes cached
Viral traffic is handled safely because the write path automatically re-shards the database the moment QPS exceeds the provisioned baseline
The design is at risk because a single hot key forces every read to bypass the cache and hit the database directly, regardless of TTL
The risk is eliminated entirely as soon as the link is created, since the cache is proactively filled using write-through caching at shorten time
explanation: A viral code is also the easiest key to cache, since once the mapping is warm in Redis (and ideally at the CDN edge under a 301), repeated identical reads are absorbed almost entirely without reaching the database. The actual danger is the thundering-herd moment right as the link starts trending and the key is still cold, which calls for pre-warming or request coalescing rather than letting every concurrent miss stampede the database.

promptText: Why would encoding a raw, unmodified auto-increment ID directly into a short code (so codes appear sequential) be a problem worth addressing, and what constraint does the fix need to respect?
options: Sequential codes leak business-sensitive volume and rate information and are trivially enumerable; the fix must apply a reversible permutation before base62-encoding so the mapping stays a deterministic, unique function of the ID instead of reintroducing hash-style collisions
Sequential codes are a problem only because base62 cannot represent numbers larger than 62^6, requiring a switch to hashing entirely
The fix requires discarding the auto-increment ID source altogether and replacing it with content-based hashing of the long URL
Sequential codes are not actually a concern for this system, since short codes are explicitly treated as non-confidential identifiers
explanation: A visibly sequential code lets an outside observer infer total link volume and creation rate from just a handful of samples, and makes the entire code space trivially enumerable and scrapeable. The fix is a reversible bit-mixing or permutation step before encoding, which must stay deterministic and collision-free — this is a distinct concern from the separate point that codes need not be unguessable for access-control purposes.

promptText: Why does the Spring implementation use a Redis-backed CacheManager for the @Cacheable redirect lookup instead of Spring's default in-memory cache?
options: Because the API service is horizontally scaled and stateless, an in-memory cache would be local to whichever instance populated it and invisible to every other instance behind the load balancer, defeating the purpose of a shared cache
Because Spring's default in-memory cache cannot be combined with an @Cacheable method that also performs a database read
Because in-memory caches do not support TTL expiration, which this read path depends on for correctness
Because Redis is required to satisfy the database-level uniqueness constraint on short_code
explanation: Because the service is stateless and horizontally scaled, an in-memory HashMap cache would only ever be visible to the one instance that populated it, so a redirect cached on one instance would be invisible to a request load-balanced onto another. A Redis-backed cache is shared across every instance, so a mapping warmed by one instance's miss benefits every other instance's subsequent lookups for the same code.

promptText: When a short code is deactivated (expired, deleted, or taken down), what must the design do beyond updating the database row, and why?
options: It must also invalidate or update the corresponding cache entry, since otherwise a recently-deactivated link could keep resolving successfully from a stale cache entry until its TTL naturally expires, even though the database already reflects deactivation
It must permanently delete the row rather than soft-deleting it, since soft-deleted rows cannot be excluded from the primary-key index
It must notify every CDN edge node synchronously before the deactivation is considered complete, blocking the operation until all nodes confirm
Nothing beyond the database update is required, since cache-aside guarantees the cache is always consistent with the database on every read
explanation: Soft-deleting via an is_active flag keeps a deactivated-versus-never-existed distinction queryable, but the cache itself must also be invalidated or updated on deactivation, not just the database row. Otherwise a stale cache entry from before deactivation can keep resolving correctly-looking but now-wrong redirects until its TTL happens to expire on its own.

promptText: An interviewer raises the required sustained write throughput from roughly 117/sec to 50,000/sec. Which combination of changes correctly follows from the chapter's stated scaling thresholds, and what new problem does it introduce?
options: ID allocation moves to a pre-generated key-pool service, the mapping table is sharded by a hash of the short code using consistent hashing, and custom-alias uniqueness becomes harder to enforce since a constraint on a sharded table can no longer guarantee global uniqueness without a separate, differently-sharded reservation mechanism
The redirect read path must be sharded first, since reads always bottleneck before writes do in a read-heavy system regardless of write volume
Switching from base62 encoding to UUIDs resolves the write-throughput bottleneck, since UUIDs require no coordinated ID source at any scale
A single database sequence comfortably absorbs 50,000 writes/second without any architectural change, since write volume was never the limiting factor in this design
explanation: At that volume, a single ID sequence and an unsharded table both cross the thresholds the chapter names for introducing a pre-generated key pool and sharding the mapping table by hash of the short code with consistent hashing. The one piece that doesn't shard cleanly is custom-alias uniqueness, since a generated code shards trivially but a user-chosen alias needs global uniqueness that sharding actively complicates, requiring a separate reservation step.

promptText: Deploying this system across multiple geographic regions for latency reasons, why is the read path straightforward to localize while the write path is the harder design question?
options: Read replicas and cache nodes per region serve the dominant read traffic locally with low complexity, but true multi-region active-active writes require either a coordinated cross-region ID-allocation scheme or an accepted conflict-resolution model, since a single centralized ID sequence would become a cross-region bottleneck
The read path is harder to localize because cache entries cannot be replicated across regions under any circumstances
The write path is trivial to localize because every region can independently run its own primary database without coordination, since writes are rare relative to reads
Both paths are equally difficult to localize because the short-code uniqueness constraint requires a single global database instance regardless of region
explanation: Because the workload is overwhelmingly read-dominant, placing read replicas and cache nodes in each region captures most of the latency win with relatively little complexity. A single-region write primary is simplest and fits the design's relaxed-consistency stance, but genuine active-active writes across regions need either partitioned ID ranges per region or an accepted conflict-resolution model, since a single centralized ID source would otherwise force cross-region coordination on every write.

promptText: The entire Redis cache layer fails completely (not just a single hot key). How does this differ in impact from the single-hot-key thundering-herd scenario, and what should the mitigation focus on?
options: Correctness is unaffected since the database remains authoritative, but now 100% of previously cache-absorbed traffic across every code lands on the database and replicas simultaneously, so mitigation centers on replica headroom and graceful degradation rather than coalescing requests for one key
A full cache outage is strictly less severe than a single hot key going viral, since total outages are rare enough that no mitigation is necessary
A full cache outage causes permanent data loss, since the database never held the mapping in the first place and relied on the cache as the system of record
The correct mitigation is identical to the hot-key case: a distributed lock around the single affected key so only one request rebuilds it while others wait
explanation: A total cache failure doesn't threaten correctness, because the database remains the ground truth and every redirect still resolves, just slower. The real exposure is a sudden, system-wide load spike as all previously cache-absorbed traffic lands on the database and replicas at once, which calls for provisioning replica headroom, graceful degradation, and a cache warm-up strategy rather than the single-key request-coalescing fix that addresses a localized hot-key stampede instead.
